stories.headline: NFL betting expected to slow at U.S. sportsbooks in 2026
stories.summary: NFL betting has grown for years, climbing to approximately $30 billion, but the boom is showing signs of stalling at U.S. sportsbooks as prediction markets gain ground.
stories.body:
NFL betting has grown for years, climbing to approximately $30 billion, but the boom is showing signs of stalling at U.S. sportsbooks as prediction markets gain ground.

The American Gaming Association estimates that $29.5 billion will be bet on the 2026 NFL season with domestic sportsbooks, up just 0.3% from last season's figure based on revenue reports from state gaming regulators.

Missouri is the only state to launch legal betting since 2025, contributing to the stalled growth of the sportsbook industry, but the rise of prediction markets is believed to be a major factor, according to the AGA.

From last September through May, the amount bet with U.S. sportsbooks grew by 4%, after having grown by 14% over the same period the previous year, according to the AGA. Last football season was the first that prediction markets such as Kalshi began offering a large menu of sports markets.

Experts expect NFL trading volume on prediction markets to double this season, potentially reaching $36.8 billion, according to analysis from Rotowire.com. Prediction market volume differs somewhat from betting handle because the contracts can change hands multiple times.

Industry research firm Eilers & Krejcik Gaming found that NFL trading volume on prediction markets in August was 4.6 times higher than last August.

Prediction markets have taken off despite legal challenges and concerns from the NFL. Last week, a federal appeals court ruled that Nevada could enforce its gaming regulations to prohibit Kalshi from offering trading on sports in the state. On Wednesday, New Jersey asked the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in on the legality of prediction markets.

The NFL sent a letter to prediction market operators this week, expressing concern that some markets being offered threaten the integrity of the sport.

"It is deeply concerning that bets within the objectionable categories that we identified months ago have been and continue to be listed as contracts on exchanges," Sabrina Perel, the NFL's chief compliance officer, wrote in the letter obtained by ESPN.

AGA CEO and president Bill Miller, in a release announcing the lobbying group's annual NFL betting estimate, accused prediction markets of "misleading" consumers, refusing to follow state and tribal sports betting laws, and avoiding gaming taxes.

"Their defiance means consumers, including teenagers and freshmen, placing bets without the protections, oversight and accountability that the legal market provides," Miller said.

Prediction markets allow customers 18 or older to trade, while the legal age for regulated sportsbooks is 21 in most states. The Coalition for Prediction Markets did not respond to a request for comment from ESPN.

The NFL season kicks off Wednesday with a Super Bowl rematch between the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots.

stories.headline: Ben Simmons returning to NBA on 1-year, $3.5M deal with Kings
stories.summary: Ben Simmons is back in the NBA after reaching one-year, $3.5 million deal with the Kings, his agents Max Wiepking, Sean Tribe and Ryan Arney told Andscape and ESPN's Shams Charania.
stories.body:
Three-time NBA All-Star Ben Simmons is back in the NBA after agreeing to a one-year, $3.5 million contract with the Sacramento Kings on Friday, his agents Max Wiepking, Sean Tribe and Ryan Arney told Andscape and ESPN's Shams Charania.

Simmons returns to the NBA after missing the 2025-26 season to rehabilitate lingering back and leg injuries. Now healthy, the 6-foot-10, 240-pounder impressed Kings general manager Scott Perry when he worked out for him in Miami and had an hourlong meeting in late August.

Simmons also traveled to Sacramento to visit the Kings and impressed head coach Doug Christie and other members of the basketball staff at the team's practice facility on Monday where he underwent an in-depth medical exam, conducted an on-court workout and met with the entire coaching staff.

In the following days, the Kings offered Simmons a contract with the expectation of him being a backup point guard for rookie Darius Acuff Jr. and play positions one through five. For the Kings, Simmons serves as a high-upside reclamation project who still has years left in his perspective prime.

Simmons' stock rose after he played well while being a full participant in a minicamp with the Australia men's basketball national team in early August. The Minnesota Timberwolves and the Golden State Warriors expressed interest in Simmons that could have led to a potential training camp invite. The Kings, however, were the only NBA team to offer him contract. A source said Simmons is excited about playing for the Kings and believes the organization will give him the support and opportunity he has hoped for in his return to the NBA.

The Kings finished 22-60 last season, tying for the worst record in the Western Conference. They waived DeMar DeRozan in July and didn't bring back free agent Russell Westbrook, leaving them with a hole at the guard position.

Simmons was the first overall pick by the Philadelphia 76ers in the 2016 NBA draft out of LSU. The Melbourne, Australia, native won the 2018 NBA Rookie of the Year award and was an NBA All-Defensive first-team selection in 2020.

The 30-year-old's NBA career has also included numerous challenges, including missing the 2016-17 season with a foot injury, missing the entire 2021-22 NBA season amid a trade holdout, mental health concerns and various physical ailments.

Simmons has averaged 13.1 points, 7.4 rebounds, 7.2 assists and 1.5 steals in 383 regular-season games for the 76ers, the Brooklyn Nets and the LA Clippers. After being waived following a buyout with the Nets on Feb. 8, 2025, Simmons averaged 2.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 3.1 assists with the Clippers while playing limited minutes and fighting back issues in 18 games last season.

Simmons' last NBA game was Game 5 of the 2025 Western Conference first-round playoffs on April 29, 2025, while playing for the Clippers against the Denver Nuggets. He told Andscape in July that he felt as healthy as he had in years and believed he was ready to return to the NBA.

During his NBA hiatus, he purchased a 50% ownership stake in the South Florida Sails professional angling club in December 2025, becoming the team's controlling operator.

stories.headline: Mikel Arteta happy with Arsenal 'intention' in transfer market despite Vinícius Júnior, Julián Álvarez snubs
stories.summary: Mikel Arteta has insisted Arsenal showed enough ambition in the transfer market this summer despite missing out on signing a top class forward.
stories.body:
Mikel Arteta has insisted Arsenal showed enough ambition in the transfer market this summer despite missing out on signing a top class forward.

The Gunners were willing to make Vinícius Júnior their highest-paid player before the Brazil winger chose to sign a new contract with Real Madrid, while they ultimately failed to convince Julián Álvarez to leave Atlético Madrid.

Sources have told ESPN that Arsenal also held a firm interest in Morgan Rogers but were reluctant to pay Aston Villa's asking price, only for Chelsea to swiftly agree a £117 million ($158m) deal last month.

The Gunners spent £200m on five new signings with Bruno Guimarães, Ezri Konsa, Christos Tzolis and Illan Meslier while making Piero Hincapié's loan move from Bayer Leverkusen permanent.

Arteta stated after the club's Champions League Final defeat to Paris Saint-Germain in May that Arsenal needed to be "very ambitious, very fast and very smart" in the market and when asked if their summer window had satisfied that criteria, he said: "Yeah, 100%. The outcome after can be different to what you expect but the intention is certainly there which is in my opinion what I value the most.

"It doesn't depend on you only. I think Andrea [Berta, sporting director] is better, or Josh [Kronke, co-chariman], to talk about that [how hard those deals are to do], because I am not in those negotiations. They know much better than me. These are questions that are related to the market and all aspects that I think it is better they speak about it."

- Martinelli joins Al Hilal from Arsenal for £60m

- Arsenal lack '10 out of 10' attacker - Carragher

- Ranked: The 11 transfers from this summer most likely to fail

When it was put to Arteta that prices for players had increased, he replied "it looks like it" before adding: "I'm sure that when this happens, it is because there has been an analysis behind it that this is going to be sustainable and other resources will appear, or the valuation of every player will be then much higher and it will be done in a sustainable way.

"But again, that is something for the Premier League and the owners to look at and evaluate."

Arteta revealed that Bruno Guimarães picked up a knock against Aston Villa but is expected to train on Saturday, when Cristhian Mosquera will also be checked over after he was substituted at Villa Park with a muscular issue as a precaution.

stories.headline: Alpine's Pierre Gasly stripped of Monaco GP podium after McLaren and Red Bull win appeal
stories.summary: Pierre Gasly's penalties from the Monaco Grand Prix have been reinstated 89 days after the race, meaning he has lost the podium to Isack Hadjar a second time.
stories.body:
Pierre Gasly's penalties from the Monaco Grand Prix have been reinstated 89 days on from the race, meaning he has lost the podium to Isack Hadjar for a second time.

Gasly finished third on the grid during June's grand prix but was immediately demoted to seventh position when two 10-second time penalties issued to him for incidents in the race were applied.

That elevated Hadjar to third and McLaren's Oscar Piastri up to fourth, with Racing Bulls pair Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad fifth and sixth, respectively -- that order has now been confirmed as the official outcome of the race.

Friday's verdict gives Hadjar his second F1 grand prix podium and his first since joining Red Bull this year.

Gasly was one of five drivers to have been given penalties for minor speeding infractions in the pit lane -- he had entered the pits 0.1 km/h and 0.4 km/h over the 60 km/h limit on two visits.

Gasly's penalties immediately shuffled him down the order, losing him and Alpine the podium and nine championship points.

Alpine was able to successfully protest the result a week later, with his penalties removed and his place on the podium reestablished ahead of the following week's Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix.

Alpine had put forward a case that the FIA's system used to measure speed on pit entry had been flawed, an argument that was accepted.

However, Red Bull, McLaren and Racing Bulls then protested that decision. On Friday, the FIA's International Court of Appeal -- independent of the FIA's sporting and regulatory administration -- threw out the verdict of Alpine's appeal, which the FIA itself also defended.

In a statement issued immediately after the FIA's 26-page verdict document was released on Friday, Alpine said: "The team expresses its disappointment and frustration with the outcome reached by the FIA International Court of Appeal relating to the result of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

"While we disagree with the decision, and still fully maintain that Car 10 did not exceed the Pit Lane speed limit at any point during the race, the team acknowledges the decision of the judging panel from the recent hearing in Paris.

"While the result is not what we had hoped for, as we feel that we have been unjustly punished, the team is firmly focused on continuing to improve its performance on track and remains in a close and very competitive Championship fight. This outcome will not deter the team's efforts and motivation in achieving its objectives by the end of the season."

- Monza personifies the passion that enticed Leclerc to commit his future to Ferrari

- Lando Norris says he would be 'proud' if he finished his F1 career with McLaren

- Italian Grand Prix declared heat hazard; second race this season

Gasly had been "heartbroken" immediately after crossing the line as the realization dawned on him that he would lose the spot on the podium of F1's famous street race.

The French driver and his team had been convinced there were issues with the measuring system used to judge entry speed at the tight right-hand pit lane before the final corner.

After the race, Alpine was granted an appeal hearing after meeting the criteria for presenting the FIA with new, relevant and significant information not available to the stewards at the time, which is required under the rules to force a proper appeal process.

In the follow-up hearing, the FIA deemed that Gasly did not exceed the 60 km/h speed limit. The stewards accepted new evidence -- including evidence provided by Formula One Management -- that the official measurement used for calculating the pit lane speed was incorrect.

This evidence showed the distance used to calculate speeds in the first pit lane timing zone was longer than the shortest route actually available to drivers following changes to the curved pit entry layout.

Monaco's official timing system used a distance of 26.92 meters between timing loops to judge speed, and Alpine pointed out that a shorter theoretical distance of 26.15 meters actually existed, which could skew speed measurements. The FIA supported Alpine's case in front of the FIA's International Court of Appeal, but the logic was dismissed on the grounds of sporting fairness.

The court reasoned that Alpine's postrace evidence was not enough to prove Gasly was not speeding -- by the time measurements were taken, Monaco's circuit had already started being dismantled and the configuration could not be re-created exactly.

Alpine had called its own measurements a "best estimate."

Importantly, the International Court of Appeal did not state that Alpine's measurements had been incorrect, but rather that it could not be proved that it was completely accurate beyond any shadow of a doubt.

It was also reasoned that rival teams had calibrated their own pit limiters and driven the weekend by the same benchmark, even if the measurement itself was flawed, and had stayed within the speed allowed.

One of the other cars that had picked up penalties was Gasly's Alpine teammate, Franco Colapinto. The International Court of Appeal pointed out that "no other party petitioned for Right of Review within the allowable time frame."

Mercedes had weighed up an appeal of its own as George Russell had been dropped out of the points with a time penalty for a pit lane speeding infraction.

However, Russell and Mercedes' decision to serve the penalty in the race meant it could not be overturned anyway. On this, Friday's verdict stated of Russell's situation that "there will undoubtedly remain questions as to whether those breaches were genuine."

Gasly and Alpine's initial appeal had been admissible because their penalty had been applied in the form of a time penalty at the conclusion of the race.

The FIA's International Court of Appeal ordered the FIA and Alpine to split the costs of the process, rejecting the FIA's defense of the stewards' decision.

stories.headline: Will Shohei Ohtani pitch in October? 5 questions for Los Angeles Dodgers
stories.summary: Ohtani hasn't been healthy enough to pitch in two months. Is his value as a pitcher in the postseason worth risking his bat?
stories.body:
Shohei Ohtani was noticeably uncomfortable when he took his last at-bat in Wednesday's 10th inning. He swung through a Riley O'Brien slider with a noticeable lack of support from his lower half. As he retreated to the dugout -- in the wake of his fourth strikeout of the night, with his Los Angeles Dodgers on their way to a sixth loss in eight games -- he shook his right arm.

To some Dodgers officials, it was the first clear sign that the ailments preventing Ohtani from pitching for two months were bleeding into his at-bats. To Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, it was "the tip of the iceberg."

Ohtani was held out of the Dodgers' lineup on Thursday, his first absence since July 30, and described as day-to-day. A stint on the injured list seems unlikely. The hope is that one or two days off will be enough for Ohtani's body to recover to at least be unencumbered offensively. But the other side of his game lingers.

Ohtani has not pitched in a game since July 3 and has not thrown off a mound in seven days, when last Friday's bullpen session -- a potential precursor to him rejoining the Dodgers' rotation -- was cut short due to lingering soreness in his left knee and right bicep.

With the postseason less than a month away, the Dodgers face a major dilemma around whether to keep Ohtani's two-way ambitions viable for the stretch run. Eliminating the possibility of him pitching in October is not a decision the Dodgers will arrive at easily. He's that valuable on the mound, even in a limited capacity. If it's obvious that continuing to pursue pitching is impacting his offense, then their decision to shut him down as a pitcher will be simple. But that's something the team's principal decision-makers have yet to determine.

As is often the case with the most unique player in baseball history, the path is not straightforward.

Below are the five biggest questions for the Dodgers to consider when it comes to Ohtani's role for the final stretch of their season.

What do the Dodgers need most from Ohtani -- pitching or hitting?
Roberts left no doubt when asked that very question over the weekend.

"His value offensively is hugely important," he said of Ohtani, "and so we can't compromise that in any fashion."

Without Ohtani, the Dodgers would still possess arguably the best postseason rotation in baseball. They have Tarik Skubal, the reigning two-time American League Cy Young Award winner; Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who dazzled last fall and has put together another brilliant season; Blake Snell, who has pitched to a 1.17 ERA in four starts since coming off the injured list; and Tyler Glasnow, who has been just as sharp in his return from the IL.

The Dodgers' offense is every bit as decorated -- but nowhere near as productive.

Since the start of July, Dodgers hitters rank 22nd in OPS (.703), 23rd in runs per game (4.2) and 22nd in weighted runs created plus (94). Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernandez and Tommy Edman all slumped in August. Freddie Freeman went 47 games without homering before finally going deep again on Wednesday. And after posting the worst offensive season of his career last year, Mookie Betts has been even worse in 2026.

In other words: It's easy for the Dodgers to envision themselves winning a championship without getting any innings from Ohtani in October, a time of year when only four starting pitchers are required. But it's almost impossible to see them winning it all if he's not himself offensively. It's why Roberts said he's "very, very bullish on making sure we don't compromise the hitting."

Does pitching typically impact Ohtani's hitting -- and, if so, how?
This question has long been debated by the Dodgers, even when he's fully healthy. There are some who don't believe there's any meaningful correlation, while others -- players included -- believe the toll of pitching absolutely plays a part in Ohtani's offensive production.

The numbers are inconclusive.

If you go back to 2023, his last year as a full-time two-way player, Ohtani slashed .372/.490/.731 on his start days with the Angels. When he slumped last July, after settling into the rotation in the wake of his second elbow surgery, it raised eyebrows. But then he dominated in August and September, putting up a 1.091 OPS while his workload as a starter increased. On his start days this year, he has slashed .250/.372/.500. When playing the day after his start days, something the Dodgers have been trying to avoid, he slashed .250/.478/.500. On all other days, he has slashed .288/.383/.542.

Health changes that dynamic entirely.

"If you're not a hundred percent, there's possibly some bleed-in to the performance offensively," Roberts told reporters on Wednesday. "That's just me kind of theorizing."

Ohtani's recent slump -- seven hits and 20 strikeouts in his past 51 at-bats -- certainly lends credence to that theory. For much of that stretch, the Dodgers viewed it as a relatively small sample size that was more a product of bad pitch selection and just one of the typical lulls Ohtani will have in any given season. Leading up to this week, Ohtani had not expressed any discomfort to the Dodgers' trainers and coaches while hitting, according to Roberts.

Then came Wednesday's last swing, in which Ohtani experienced soreness on the right side of his neck and down through his arm.

It could change the dynamic entirely.

How much pain is Ohtani in?
"If any pitcher was feeling like this, we wouldn't run him out there," Roberts said when he announced Ohtani would not start on Sunday.

That's a pretty clear indication that he's not all that close.

Ohtani spent much of June managing pain in his left knee -- while still putting up a 1.091 OPS -- before finally agreeing to take a break from pitching. That it has been two months and the pain remains, even after the relatively light work of a 20-pitch bullpen session, is concerning.

Ohtani has tried to make adjustments with the position of his landing leg to ease some of the irritation in that left knee -- the same knee that was operated on to address a rare congenital condition called a bipartite patella in 2019 -- but they clearly have not worked. The right biceps issue that flared up on him several weeks ago has also resurfaced.

At this point, it would be a matter of pain tolerance -- but because he performs two roles, it's a lot more complicated.

"I just don't see everything getting to 100% by the end of the season," Roberts said of Ohtani, who has not addressed the media since Aug. 17. "But there's a lot of pitchers that are not 100% and still viable. It's just not an exact science."

What about running the bases?
As a two-way player for the Angels, Ohtani stole 57 bases from 2021 to 2023. In 2024, when he was strictly the Dodgers' designated hitter, he stole 59. By the end of April 2025, he had racked up nine steals, four shy of the major league lead.

Then Ohtani started to build up as a pitcher, and he just stopped running.

Ohtani made just 16 stolen-base attempts over the past five months of the 2025 regular season, 11 of them successfully. He has attempted 14 steals all of his year, including zero in June and July. So while there might be ambiguity over how Ohtani's hitting is impacted by his pitching, there is no doubt that his baserunning takes a backseat when he's juggling a two-way role.

Since May 2025, Ohtani has been worth 3.6 baserunning runs above average, still good enough to rank 25th among qualifiers; his speed and acumen still show up when opportunities to take extra bases present themselves. In 2024, though, Ohtani was worth 9.8 baserunning runs above average, second most in the majors.

Would putting a pause on pitching unlock this version of Ohtani for the stretch run and into the playoffs? It's safe to say he'd become more aggressive on the bases, to some extent. But how much does that really matter in the postseason, a time of year when runs are at a premium and teams are far less likely to risk getting thrown out on stolen-base attempts? And is it enough to sacrifice the potential impact of him on the mound?

As one high-ranking Dodgers official put it: "Absolutely not."

Is it worth it to keep his October pitching hopes alive?
It's clear at this point that Ohtani doesn't have enough time to build up as a traditional starting pitcher for the playoffs, and yet, he hasn't been shut down as a pitcher. There's a clear reason for that:

Even a handful of innings in the playoffs is exceedingly valuable.

Keep in mind Ohtani doesn't count as an extra pitcher, which means keeping him as an option won't cost the Dodgers anything. If he can, say, open for Glasnow as a way for the Dodgers to lessen the amount of innings that would have to be covered by their bullpen, that's a major plus. Or let's say it's the ninth inning of a decisive game and the Dodgers lead by a run or two. Having Ohtani in their back pocket -- in a world where Edwin Díaz still hasn't worked out of his struggles and Roki Sasaki is still troubled by a blister -- is invaluable.

Scenarios like that don't necessarily require firm timetables. Ohtani can continue to take his time, keep his arm active -- he's still working with plyometric training balls, even if he isn't currently playing catch -- and basically be available for that type of work, so long as he's throwing off a mound again before the end of September. Still, Roberts said Wednesday that shutting Ohtani down as a pitcher is "an option."

It's a decision that won't be made without Ohtani's blessing.

"It's his decision, honestly," Roberts said. "If he feels like he's capable, then we'll run the play out until it doesn't make any sense."

stories.headline: Taylor Harwood-Bellis left out of Aston Villa Champions League squad after expressing 'excitement' for 'biggest stage'
stories.summary: Taylor Harwood-Bellis was omitted from Aston Villa's squad for the Champions League, two days after arriving at the club and explaining his ambition to play in the tournament.
stories.body:
Taylor Harwood-Bellis was omitted from Aston Villa's squad for the Champions League, two days after arriving at the club and explaining his ambition to play in the tournament.

Harwood-Bellis signed for Villa on Tuesday, the Premier League's transfer deadline day, from Championship side Southampton.

He said upon arrival: "The club, in general, being such a prestigious Premier League club. And then you have the added bonus of the Champions League -- it doesn't fill me with anything but excitement.

"I can't get wait to get out there and show that I can hopefully do it on the biggest stage.

"We've seen the success that the club has had in Europe, winning the Europa League and going so far in the Champions League. I know that the club can relish in Europe as well."

However, that dream will be postponed until at least later this season because Villa's squad for the league phase of Europe's top competition did not include the defender.

If Unai Emery's side qualify from the league phase into the knockout stages they will submit a fresh squad which Harwood-Bellis could be added to.

stories.headline: How the US basketball system has shaped Nigeria's D'Tigress
stories.summary: The United States basketball system has played a major role in the development of Nigeria's national women's basketball team, known as D'Tigress.
stories.body:
The United States basketball system has played a major role in the development of Nigeria's national women's basketball team, known as D'Tigress.

Several players in Nigeria's FIBA Women's World Cup pool were born or developed in the USA, went through the NCAA system, or have connections to the WNBA.

Protland Fire's Amy Okonkwo began her college career at USC before transferring to TCU, where she became the Big 12 Sixth Player of the Year.

Ezinne Kalu played at Savannah State, finishing her career as the first player in program history to score more than 2,000 points.

Elizabeth Balogun's college career took her through Georgia Tech, Louisville and Duke. She was named ACC Freshman of the Year at Georgia Tech and reached the Elite Eight with Louisville before completing her college career at Duke.

Pallas Kunaiyi-Akpanah played four seasons at Northwestern, developing into one of the Big Ten's leading rebounders before spending time with the Chicago Sky.

Promise Amukamara played at Arizona State, while Enabosi starred at Delaware.

Head coach Rena Wakama has connections to both levels herself. She played college basketball at Western Carolina and is now an assistant with the Chicago Sky.

Those ties were evident during Nigeria's World Cup preparation, when D'Tigress played exhibitions against three WNBA teams, the Los Angeles Sparks, Minnesota Lynx and Indiana Fever, before continuing their preparations in China and Europe.

Ezinne Kalu
If there is a heartbeat to this D'Tigress team, it is Kalu. The 34-year-old point guard is the most experienced major-tournament player in Nigeria's current pool, having played at the 2018 World Cup, the Tokyo and Paris Olympics and four Women's AfroBaskets.

Kalu produced arguably the best basketball of her international career in Paris, averaging 18.5 points, four assists and three rebounds in four games.

She remains Nigeria's primary playmaker. At the World Cup qualifying tournament in March, Kalu averaged 9.4 points, 4.8 assists and 2.2 steals per game.

As the team head to Berlin, she is calling for Nigerians in Germany to give D'Tigress something approaching home support.

"We are heading to Berlin for the World Cup, and we need our people there to support us," Kalu said in an Instagram post.

"So we need every Nigerian near Berlin to come through. Bring your flag, your voice and energy."

Amy Okonkwo
Okonkwo has established herself as one of the best players, if not the best, in African basketball. The 6-foot-2 forward has won consecutive Women's AfroBasket MVP awards after leading Nigeria to the 2023 and 2025 championships.

The WNBA player averaged 14 points and six rebounds at the 2025 tournament and scored 19 points while playing all 40 minutes of the final against Mali.

Her ability to score inside, stretch defenses from the perimeter and rebound gives coach Rena Wakama one of her most versatile offensive options.

Berlin will be Okonkwo's World Cup debut, but hardly her first experience at this level. She played at both the Tokyo and Paris Olympics and has been a central figure in Nigeria's last two AfroBasket championships.

At club level, she has traversed Europe, and has also held her own with short but remarkable stints in the WNBA with Dallas Wings, Atlanta Dream and currently Portland.

Victoria Macaulay
The veteran center, who was born in New York, was arguably Nigeria's best performer during the March qualifying tournament. She averaged a team-leading 13.6 points and produced a team-best 16.4 efficiency rating over five games.

The Temple grad brings considerable international experience despite never having played at a World Cup, having represented Nigeria at the Tokyo Olympics and at the 2019 and 2025 AfroBaskets.

Alongside Musa and Pallas Kunaiyi-Akpanah, she gives Nigeria size, experience and physicality in the frontcourt.

Elizabeth Balogun
Balogun could be one of Nigeria's most intriguing players in Berlin. The guard averaged 10.6 points during the qualifying tournament and then produced one of the standout performances of Nigeria's World Cup preparation, scoring 26 points in an 88-77 victory over China in August.

Like Okonkwo, Balogun will be making her World Cup debut despite already having significant global tournament experience. She represented Nigeria at both Tokyo and Paris and was part of the 2023 and 2025 AfroBasket championship teams.

Balogun has also added another American professional connection to the roster after signing a development-player contract with the New York Liberty.

stories.headline: What we learned: Pressure can win Hawks the flag; the massive warning sign for Freo
stories.summary: The Hawks' outstanding pressure can win them a premiership, but the Dockers have a big problem after a 'morale-sapping' home qualifying final loss. Here's three things we learned from Hawthorn's win over Fremantle.
stories.body:
Hawthorn produced a stunning performance Thursday evening at Optus Stadium to upset minor premier Fremantle and advance to a second successive preliminary final.

Sam Mitchell's side will now enjoy the week off before returning to the MCG to hunt a place in the 2026 AFL Grand Final. Meanwhile, the Dockers will face the winner of Geelong and Carlton next week in a must-win semifinal.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

Hawthorn's relentless pressure can win the flag
It was a masterclass of pressure and intensity from the Hawks on Thursday evening in the west as they put the Dockers to the sword on their home deck to book their ticket to the final four once again.

The Hawks played the wet-dry conditions perfectly and completely stymied the minor premiers for four quarters. Sam Mitchell's side brought the heat from the opening siren, pressing up and hunting in packs, while never allowing their opponents a moment to breathe and settle into the contest.

They locked the ball inside their attacking forward 50 and had Fremantle's back six under siege for most of the evening, forcing the Dockers into 32 defensive half turnovers -- their most in a game all year. Neither the Docker defense, nor the midfield group, had any answers to stop the onslaught as they again buckled under the finals spotlight.

Mabior Chol set the standard in the opening minutes with two gut-busting efforts inside forward 50. His fleet-footed brigade of small forwards never stood still for a second, while co-captain Jai Newcombe and Dylan Moore were in-and-under all night long, combining for 14 tackles.

It was this insatiable intent and appetite for the contest that allowed Hawthorn to pile on six consecutive goals following Luke Jackson's early opener. The Hawks took a 33-point advantage into the main break, restricting Fremantle to that lone Jackson major. The margin remained the same at the final change and could only be cut to 32 by the final siren.

Thursday's performance was proof the stat sheet can sometimes be a tad misleading. The Dockers dominated total disposals (+74) and enjoyed an advantage in inside 50s (+6), while the clearance and contested possession counts were virtually identical. And yet this game only ever looked like having one victor.

Hawthorn will now enjoy a well-earned week off before returning to the MCG for a preliminary final. The three most likely opponents for that game all reside outside Victoria. If the home crowd support can be paired with the ferocity displayed against Fremantle, there's no reason they can't jag two more wins in 2026.

We should be seriously worried about these Dockers
Fremantle had been the team of the season. Minor premiers with 19 wins and four losses. An even more imposing record at Optus Stadium where they were unbeaten in 12 games, including a sensational come-from-behind win against these Hawks back in Round 9.

Unfortunately for Justin Longmuir and the legion of fans decked head to toe in purple, the Dockers waited until September to turn in their biggest stinker of the year. The Hawks played this game like the final it was and the all-conquering home side never appeared close to being up for the occasion.

Aside from All-Australian running defender Jordan Clark and the reliable Andrew Brayshaw, Fremantle had few winners on the night. Midfielders Shai Bolton and Caleb Serong were well below their best, Murphy Reid left his kicking boots at home, while forward pair Josh Treacy and Jye Amiss were just about unsighted throughout.

Thursday evening was Fremantle's lowest score of the season (40), while the 17 points scored from turnover were the fewest they had managed in a game since 2019 (excluding season 2020 which featured shortened quarters). It was also the club's second-worst game of the year for converting scores from inside 50s.

Fremantle will now have to pick themselves up, dust themselves off, and regroup for a do-or-die semifinal against either Geelong or Carlton next weekend. And while they'll likely be favoured to win that game, would anyone be tipping them with a high degree of confidence?

The loss to the Hawks is as morale-sapping as it gets. Not only because it undoes so much of the great work that was done throughout the year. Not because for them to lift the premiership they'd have to win three straight games, including two on the other side of the country. But because this club, and its supporter base, was adamant it had turned the corner following last year's disappointing home elimination final defeat to Gold Coast.

That one-point loss to end last year's campaign could prove costly 12 months on. All of a sudden the Dockers have lost two finals in a row on their home deck and will be sweating at the prospect of it becoming three in a row next weekend. Meanwhile, what would the Cats or Blues really have to lose?

If you don't want James Sicily at his worst, you don't deserve him at his best
Sure, at times he can play the role of the ultimate villain, but Hawthorn co-captain James Sicily can also be the coolest head you're likely to find behind the ball and one of the greatest assets in football come September.

On Thursday evening he was very much the latter. Sicily was simply sensational against the Dockers, leading the defensive group that completely nullified Fremantle's dangerous three-pronged attack.

Time and time again Sicily out-positioned and out-bodied the Fremantle forwards, drawing on all of his experience and smarts to put on a defensive clinic. He was always in the right place at the right time, always a step ahead of his opponent, and always composed with Sherrin in hand.

Sicily finished his night in the west with a team-high 26 disposals, a game-high 12 intercept possessions, 10 marks, and seven score involvements -- more than any player wearing brown and gold not named Nick Watson.

"We wanted to commit to being tough and taking the game on," Sicily told Fox Sports after the win. "The way we were in sync tonight is just going to give us so much confidence."

There's more than a few Hawks that can make claims to being their club's most important player, but it's hard to look past Sicily when he's in this type of form.

stories.headline: Matías Galarza joins Inter Miami from River Plate
stories.summary: Matías Galarza has joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate.
stories.body:
Matías Galarza officially joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate on Thursday.

The Paraguay midfielder signed a contract with Inter Miami on Wednesday night, officially securing Galarza's move to South Florida on the final day of the MLS transfer window.

Galarza is familiar with MLS have completed a season on loan with Atlanta United FC earlier this year. He recorded one assist in 13 appearances for Atlanta across all competitions -- including MLS regular season games and U.S. Open Cup play.

Galarza also played an integral role for Paraguay at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, scoring one goal in a group stage match against Türkiye and an assist in a shocking round of 32 win over Germany.

Galarza becomes Inter Miami's second signing on deadline day, joining Brazilian winger Riquelme Fillipi, whose deal was confirmed earlier on Wednesday.

The two players join the club as new head coach Cristian Gonzalez takes over for interim manager Guillermo Hoyos.

Inter Miami made several roster moves during this window, with a source confirming to ESPN that defender Noah Allen is set to join the Chicago Fire FC. The two clubs are in advanced negotiations, with a deal set to be finalized shortly.

The MLS secondary transfer window closed at midnight on Wednesday.

Allen was absent from Inter Miami training on Wednesday morning.

Inter Miami also loaned midfielder David Ruiz to the New York Red Bulls, with the Herons receiving $75,000 in 2027 general allocation money for the deal. The Red Bulls also hold the option to make Ruiz's move permanent at the end of the current season.

Inter Miami sits in second place on the Eastern Conference table with 42 points in 22 games.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over eight seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would reset standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers such as Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the piñata while he's under contract.

We can tsk-tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player who logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent, Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL who believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's got to sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 million annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman who will be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He has a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the expected goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the expected goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this megadeal.

Winner: player empowerment
As I wrote in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players who take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

stories.headline: Straight Arrow of emotion shoots Souths to a home final
stories.summary: South Sydney will ride a wave of Jai Arrow-fuelled emotion into a home final, after easily dispatching arch-rivals Sydney Roosters 50-20 at Allianz Stadium.
stories.body:
South Sydney will ride a wave of Jai Arrow-fuelled emotion into a home final, after easily dispatching archrivals Sydney Roosters 50-20 at Allianz Stadium.

On a night when Latrell Mitchell sent a warning to the competition and David Fifita starred, the Rabbitohs hit their first half-century of the year against a Roosters side resting nine stars.

The result means Souths will almost certainly finish sixth and play Newcastle next weekend in an elimination final at either Allianz or Accor Stadium.

The Roosters are locked into fourth, and will travel to face whoever claims the minor premiership out of the Warriors or Penrith.

South Sydney's history is littered with emotion, not least of which during the club's NRL exile in 2000 and 2001, before their 2002 return.

But no season has carried this much feeling, from Alex Johnston breaking the try-scoring record and Nathan Merritt's cancer battle, to Arrow's motor neurone disease diagnosis.

Arrow has been central to the Rabbitohs' story since his announcement in May, with fundraisers in June and July preceding two brief returns over the past week.

A sold-out crowd rose for Arrow on Friday as he brought up his 100th Rabbitohs game, before he walked off ahead of kickoff for a long embrace with Wayne Bennett.

Souths have won all four of the matches set up to honour Arrow this year, with that no doubt a driving factor for finals.

Friday night was also a near-perfect warmup.

After playing 30 minutes last week in his first game since round 11, Mitchell showed signs of his damaging best at left centre for the Rabbitohs.

Three times he put Johnston into space, once resulting in a try for the winger as part of a classic left-edge Rabbitohs movement that also included Cody Walker.

Mitchell also scored late and put a monster hit on rookie half Toby Rodwell, while Walker bagged a try of his own in the second half.

Fifita was also at his powerful best, getting the Rabbitohs' first from dummy-half and finishing the night with 11 tackle busts, while Campbell Graham bagged a double.

The only downside for the Rabbitohs was Euan Aitken ending the night in a sling with a shoulder injury, after waiting 201 games to play another final after last doing so in 2015.

The Roosters weren't short on emotion either on Friday, with Spencer Leniu baiting Rabbitohs fans while coming off the field in the first half.

Leniu had just twice clashed with Keaon Koloamatangi in the space of a minute, giving away a penalty in possession after initially earning a set restart.

The Roosters prop was not brought back on by coach Trent Robinson, while Lachlan Hubner and De La Salle Va'a were sin-binned after another melee late.

Winger Daniel Tupou got through his return from a shoulder injury unscathed and scored an early try, while the Roosters youngsters turned it on briefly in the second half.

A Cody Ramsey flick pass helped send Rex Bassingthwaighte over for the first of his two tries, before Benaiah Ioelu and a rampaging Taylor Losalu put Egan Butcher over.

stories.headline: NBA 2K27 review: A fresh experience that also feels familiar
stories.summary: NBA 2K27 lets you explore the length and breadth of basketball history, with enough detail to satisfy all types of fans.
stories.body:
Any annual sports game release is under pressure to deliver a new experience while retaining the familiarity of the previous version. It can't be so easy that it bores the hardcores, nor so difficult that it scares the casuals. As Visual Concepts' newest entry in the NBA 2K series hits digital store shelves, it's a reminder that the NBA season is nearly upon us, so let's see how the NBA's signature video game series did.

So what's new?
This year's MyPlayer mode is called "Fire & Concrete," and is the story of a former high school star whose path to college basketball was upended by an early twist in his story before working his way back up. Your player's journey will take you from streetball tournaments to the G-League and up to the NBA as you complete challenges and develop your character. It's an easy-to-understand storyline with enough character moments to keep you invested.

The animations have taken a step forward in terms of improving the fluidity of layups and up-and-unders. Depending on the angle you use to attack the rim and the attributes of your player, no two layups will look quite the same, even from the same player.

While the ability to play as WNBA teams isn't new, the ability to create a woman player underwent several significant improvements. The character creation engine is built on the same one as NBA players now and features the same customization and attribute builds as the men. Additionally, you can take your woman MyPlayer to The City and even participate in coed in every game variation there.

What are the game modes?

You can play through different eras of NBA history: The Magic vs. Bird Era (1983), Jordan Era (1991), Kobe Era (2003), LeBron Era (2010) and Steph Era (2016) -- though, the LeBron Era probably hasn't ended yet? Games in each Era are complete with period-appropriate rosters, TV graphics and jerseys. If you ever wanted to see the Seattle SuperSonics take the court against the New Jersey Nets, this is your time to shine.

NBA 2K27 also takes it a step further by allowing you to create a MyPlayer and drop them into the time period of your choice. For those nostalgic for whatever they consider the "glory days" of the NBA to be, this is a fun diversion. The game uses special filters to make the game look the way it did on TV at the time. If you grew up with older generations of the NBA, this game is a trip down memory lane and does justice to the arenas, jerseys and lineups of the time.

The MyTeam mode allows you to build your team by completing challenges and acquiring player cards, a familiar sight from any of the recent editions of the game. This is a mode that will take a healthy amount of time -- and plenty of Virtual Currency (VC) -- as you continue to fine-tune your team.

MyGM is the game mode for RPG lovers. You take over as the GM of an NBA franchise and are responsible for accomplishing ownership's goals, shaping the roster in a way that gives your club the best chance to win, and keeping your players satisfied. You can choose to simulate the games or play them out.

You can also play the WNBA season, either in The W, where you take your MyPlayer to the league or in MyWNBA, in which you take over a franchise and attempt to create your own dynasty. Want to lead the Connecticut Sun to glory before they move to Houston? Here is your last chance.

The City is a returning feature from previous seasons, in which you inhabit a mini-city devoted to basketball, from practicing your skills to upgrading your look, and most notably competing online against worldwide opponents. The City is still one of the most robust offerings in the NBA 2K series, with many different angles to interact with the game of basketball. However, you need an online account with your console of choice to get the most out of this mode, or else you will routinely lock yourself out of much of its content.

Three and D

The defensive control in this game is unforgiving -- whether you play three-on-three or five-on-five. If you're not in front of your man at all times, they can blow right past you to the hoop. It might be tempting to jump passing lanes for the steal or overcommit to blocking a shot, but if you are not successful, it will lead to a defensive breakdown. If you're not on point with your defense, your opponents could make a 2026 New York Knicks-type comeback.

The revamped defensive mechanics in this game will reward aggressive players who get the timing cues right, as shot contests factor into the shooter's green zone. It's a fitting tweak, considering the cover star is the league's best shot-blocker. Though you can use the right stick to keep your hands up, that seems to slow you down. Take it from me, focus on quickness when guarding.

For those who haven't played an NBA 2K game in a while, when the shooter starts their motion, a small meter appears next to them and if you perfect the release of the ball at the top of the meter, which is green, then the shot has its best chance to connect. However, the level of green is dependent on many factors, including the shooter's skill build, the defensive ability of the nearest defender, the spot on the court and many others ... just like the real NBA. Nail your timing, and you can live by the 3-ball, just like the 2023-24 Boston Celtics. Make poor shot selections, and your run could be over early, like the 2025-26 Celtics.

So can I just pick up and play?
Yes, you can, and it's not bad. If you don't care for complex attribute builds or the side pursuits of the other modes, you can simply pick two teams -- from any era -- and get down to business. The basics of the game, such as passing and shooting, are still intuitive if you just want a back-and-forth arcade-type of experience. If your goal for the game is just an easy gameplay or party game experience, this is it.

In fact, the NBA Today mode allows you to pick from that day's real-time NBA games with up-to-date rosters if you want to play the NBA season day-by-day.

Scouting report
If you've played any NBA 2K game in previous years, you know that if you want your MyPlayer or MyTeam to keep up with the online game, you're either going to need to grind or pay for a lot of VC to keep upgrading them. For many, this could be a limiting factor.

Nonetheless, this game is a fantastic representation of the game of basketball, from the story mode to the many things to do in The City, and particularly to the detail in the NBA and WNBA modes. There are enough improvements over the previous editions to make this year's edition feel fresh, and it is easy to find yourself sinking hours into the game. We've never had an NBA simulation that has felt as realistic as this.

stories.headline: F1 to launch 2027 season with Milan festival featuring drivers, all 11 teams
stories.summary: Formula 1 will launch its 2027 season with a three-day fan festival in Milan, culminating in a major live show featuring the drivers and team principals from all 11 teams.
stories.body:
Formula 1 will launch its 2027 season with a three-day fan festival in Milan, culminating in a major live show featuring the drivers and team principals from all 11 teams.

The event will be over the course of three days and is taking place on Feb. 18-20 in Italy. It comes after a successful event that was staged ahead of the 2025 season live in London to mark the 75th anniversary of the F1 championship.

'F1 Live Milan' is set to be split into two opportunities for fans to immersive themselves into the world of F1. The first is the 'Milan Fan Festival' which will run over three days.

The second is 'F1 The Show' which will be a one-night only spectacle on Feb. 18, featuring drivers and team principals from the 11 teams on the grid, along with music and entertainment.

"We are always thinking big and pushing boundaries, and F1 Live Milan is going to be an incredible experience created with our fans at its heart," CEO of Formula 1 Stefano Domenicali said.

"We want them to feel that they are not simply watching the sport, but they are truly immersed in it. It is an important part of our ongoing ambition to bring Formula 1 closer to fans than ever before, giving them the chance to see their heroes up close and experience the energy, innovation, and emotion that make Formula 1 so unique.

"As F1 continues to reach new audiences around the world, racing will always be our soul -- but we also want to create unforgettable experiences that bring the excitement of Formula 1 to life on an even bigger scale and continue to explore what is possible.

- Monza personifies the passion that enticed Leclerc to commit his future to Ferrari

- Lando Norris says he would be 'proud' if he finished his F1 career with McLaren

- Italian Grand Prix declared heat hazard; second race this season

"Building on the extraordinary success of F1 75 in London, F1 Live Milan will transform the city into a Formula 1 festival for three unforgettable days, bringing people together from across the globe to celebrate everything they love about our sport. stories.headline: Federico Chiesa left out of Liverpool's Champions League squad
stories.summary: Federico Chiesa has been left out of the squad sheet submitted by Liverpool for this year's UEFA Champions League league phase.
stories.body:
Federico Chiesa has been left out of Liverpool's squad for the league phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The Italy international is joined by Wataru Endo among those omitted by new boss Andoni Iraola.

Liverpool confirmed their squad ahead of the start of their European campaign against Atlético Madrid at Anfield on Sept. 9.

Both players will be unavailable for the league phase unless Liverpool are able to make a permitted change to their squad, normally injury related.

UEFA rules limit sides to a 25-player List A, with eight places reserved for 'locally trained' players, of which four must have been at the club for three seasons between the ages of 15 and 21.

Younger players can be registered separately on List B if they meet UEFA's age and development requirements, but Chiesa and Endo are not eligible.

The 28-year-old misses out with summer arrival Víctor Muñoz included, alongside Conor Bradley, who is continuing his rehabilitation from a knee injury in February. Giovanni Leoni, who suffered an ACL tear in September 2025, is also on the list.

Chiesa is currently out with a muscle injury, though a long-term absence is not expected.

Endo made only eight Premier League appearances in 2025-26, seven of them from the bench, while he featured just once in Liverpool's run to the Champions League quarterfinals.

- Lindop: Liverpool needed to add depth in the transfer window. They didn't get it

- Andoni Iraola: Bradley Barcola could make Liverpool debut against Ipswich

- Champions League draw: Good games for Liverpool, bad for Barcelona

The Reds will play eight fixtures at this stage of the competition, with home games against Atlético, Porto, Villarreal and Lens.

They will travel to face Austrian side LASK, Fenerbahce, Club Brugge and Inter Milan.

Liverpool have instead included injured forward Hugo Ekitike in their squad despite the Frenchman currently being sidelined.

As expected, Ekitike's compatriot Bradley Barcola is on the list after his move from Paris Saint-Germain, worth up to £123 million ($166 million).

stories.headline: Nigeria's D'Tigress at the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup - Everything You Need to Know
stories.summary: Nigeria's D'Tigress head to the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin as a team with an unusual combination of tournament experience and World Cup unfamiliarity.
stories.body:
Nigeria's D'Tigress head to the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin as a team with an unusual combination of global tournament experience and World Cup unfamiliarity.

Nigeria arrive as five-time defending African champions and the No. 8-ranked team in the FIBA world rankings, looking to improve on their best World Cup finish, an eighth-place showing in 2018.

The expanded 16-team World Cup runs from September 4 through13, with Nigeria drawn in Group B alongside France, South Korea and Hungary.

Here is everything you need to know about D'Tigress in Berlin.

How they qualified
Nigeria booked their place in Berlin by winning the 2025 FIBA Women's AfroBasket in Abidjan, defeating Mali 78-64 in the final to claim a fifth consecutive continental championship.

No country had previously won five consecutive Women's AfroBasket titles, and Nigeria's victory extended an unbeaten run in the competition that dates to 2015. D'Tigress have now won 29 consecutive AfroBasket games.

Ezinne Kalu led Nigeria with 20 points in the final, while Portland fire's Amy Okonkwo scored 19 as D'Tigress recovered from a slow start to pull away in the second half.

Okonkwo, who averaged 14 points and six rebounds during the tournament, was named MVP for the second consecutive AfroBasket.

Nigeria subsequently competed at the World Cup qualifying tournament in Lyon-Villeurbanne in March despite already having secured qualification as African champions.

They finished 2-3, beating Colombia 70-37 and the Philippines 101-84, while losing to South Korea 77-60, France 93-86 and Germany 81-73.

Those results carry additional significance into Berlin. Two of the teams that beat Nigeria in France, South Korea and France, have been drawn in their World Cup group.

Previous World Cup appearances
For all their success in Africa, D'Tigress have relatively little World Cup history. Berlin will be only Nigeria's third appearance at the tournament, with their tournament debut coming 20 years ago in Brazil in 2006, when they lost all five games.

It took another 12 years for them to make their breakthrough. At the 2018 World Cup in Spain, D'Tigress beat Turkey 74-68 for their first victory at the competition. They followed that by beating Argentina before defeating Greece in the qualification game to become the first African team to reach the Women's World Cup quarterfinals.

Their run ended against eventual champions the United States, but their eighth-place finish remains Nigeria's best at a World Cup.

Nigeria qualified for the 2022 tournament in Australia but did not participate after the Nigerian government withdrew the country's basketball teams from international competition amid a long-running leadership dispute within the Nigeria Basketball Federation.

That means Berlin will mark D'Tigress' return to the World Cup for the first time in eight years.

African dominance to global contenders
Nigeria's status in international basketball has changed considerably since their 2018 World Cup run. D'Tigress have won every Women's AfroBasket they have entered since 2017, claiming championships in 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025.

The biggest evidence that their dominance could translate beyond Africa came at the Paris Olympics, when they became the first African basketball team, men's or women's, to make the Olympic quarterfinals before losing to the juggernaut that is Team USA.

On the plus side, that run pushed them into the FIBA women's world top 10 for the first time and they enter Berlin ranked No. 8.

Sadly they failed to build on that when they were withdrawn from the very next Games, the 2022 tournament in Australia.

But they have come storming back and while a return to the World Cup quarterfinals would match the achievement of the 2018 team, going further would take D'Tigress into territory no African women's, or even men's team have previously reached.

The Rena Wakama effect
Nigeria's rise has become closely associated with Rena Wakama.

Wakama became the first female coach to win the Women's AfroBasket when she led Nigeria to the 2023 championship and followed it with another title in 2025.

Between those championships came Paris. Nigeria's aggressive defense became one of the stories of the Olympic tournament, with D'Tigress applying pressure across the floor, forcing turnovers and turning those mistakes into transition opportunities.

After winning her first AfroBasket in 2023, Wakama recalled the moment she realized how much resilience she had in the team.

"Against Mozambique, we were down by 10 or 12 points," she said. "I looked into their eyes, and they told me: 'Coach, we're not going to lose this game.' And they came back to win."

Wakama's preparation for Berlin has been unusual because she has had to combine the national-team job with her role as an assistant coach with the WNBA's Chicago Sky.

Earlier this year, Wakama said the qualifying tournament in France was part of a broader process of testing Nigeria against the level of opposition they will encounter at the World Cup.

"Our preparations have been intense, and this tournament here in Lyon is an important part of that process," Wakama said.

"It gives us the opportunity to test ourselves against strong competition and evaluate where we're as a team."
